This section outlines how we value nature-based recreation as an ecosystem service.

Recreation ecosystem services are the benefits people get from using natural areas for leisure, exercise and tourism. We distinguish two kinds of nature-based recreation. **Recreation from home** covers visits to natural areas by residents travelling from where they live. **Recreation from lodging** covers visits by tourists staying in accommodation, along with the accommodation and air travel those trips require. Both depend on the quality of natural ecosystems and on how easy they are to reach.

Within the SEEA EA framework, this service is a final, non-material ecosystem service:

> "Recreation-related services are contributions of ecosystems, in particular through their biophysical characteristics and qualities, that enable people to use and enjoy the environment through direct, in situ, physical and experiential interactions with the environment. These include services both to locals and to non-locals (i.e. visitors, including tourists). Recreation-related services may also be supplied to those engaging in recreational fishing or hunting. These are final ecosystem services."
[@un2021seea]

# Methods

Recreation value is the sum of four components. Each one is valued in the same way, as a quantity times a price times a nature-attribution share ($\lambda$). The value is measured in the capital-account sense, as price times quantity. It is not consumer surplus.

$$
V = \underbrace{Q^{\text{home}} p^{\text{ground}}}_{\text{daily trips}} + \underbrace{Q^{\text{lodging}} p^{\text{ground}}}_{\text{tourist trips}} + s^{\text{personal}} \lambda \underbrace{N \, p^{\text{hotel}}}_{\text{accommodation}} + s^{\text{personal}} \lambda \underbrace{A \, s^{\text{air}} p^{\text{fare}}}_{\text{air travel}}
$$

| Component | Quantity | Price | $\lambda$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recreation from home | Visits from residents to high-quality nature sites within 50 km | Round-trip fuel cost | 1 |
| Recreation from lodging | Visits from overnight tourists to high-quality nature sites within 50 km | Round-trip fuel cost | 1 |
| Accommodation | Overnight stays (UNWTO) | Hotel price per person per night | 0.183 × personal share |
| Air travel | International arrivals by origin region × share arriving by air | Regional round-trip airfare (2019 USD) | 0.183 × personal share |

: Summary of valuation components {#tbl-components}

All values are in 2019 USD. Results are reported for 250 countries and territories. @fig-overview shows the workflow.

## Estimating Quantity

There are four quantities: the visits that make up the two ground-travel components (recreation from home and from lodging), the overnight stays that accommodation is priced on, and the international arrivals that air travel is priced on. Visits require a map of recreation sites and a demand model. Overnight stays and arrivals come directly from UNWTO statistics.

### Recreation Sites

**Environmental index.** We score how attractive each landscape is for recreation by giving each ESA-CCI land cover class a score [@ESA2017LandCoverCCI]. The scores are adapted from CORINE-based scores [@Vallecillo2019196].

| LULC Class | Score |
|------------|-------|
| Cropland | 0.4 |
| Forest | 1.0 |
| Grassland | 0.7 |
| Other Natural | 0.85 |
| Water | 1.0 |
| Urban | 0.05 |
| Other | 0.0 |
| Protected Areas | 1.0 |

: Environmental index scores {#tbl-environmental}

$$\text{Environmental Score} = \sum(\text{LULC share} \times \text{LULC score}) + (\text{Protected Area share} \times 1.0)$$

The scores are then grouped into four environmental quality classes (0–3).

**Accessibility index.** Accessibility combines road density (GRIP4) [@Meijer2018] with urban share [@ESA2017LandCoverCCI].

| Category | Share of Urban | Road Density (m/km²) |
|----------|----------------|----------------------|
| High | (0.9, 1) | (100000, ∞) |
| Medium-High | (0.5, 0.9] | (33819, 100000] |
| Medium | (0.1, 0.5] | (13326, 33819] |
| Medium-Low | (0.001, 0.1] | (5453, 13326] |
| Low | [0, 0.001) | [0, 5453) |

: Accessibility index thresholds {#tbl-accessibility}

| Urban Score | Low | Medium-Low | Medium | Medium-High | High |
|-------------|-----|------------|--------|-------------|------|
| **Low** | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| **Medium-Low** | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| **Medium** | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | 5 |
| **Medium-High** | 3 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| **High** | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 5 |

: Urban-road accessibility matrix (columns are road score) {#tbl-urban-road}

**High-quality sites.** The two indices are combined into a site ranking. Pixels ranked 9 are high-quality recreation sites: they combine the highest environmental class with medium-high or high accessibility.

| Accessibility Score | Low | Medium-Low | Medium-High | High |
|---------------------|-----|------------|-------------|------|
| **Low** | 1 | 1 | 4 | 7 |
| **Medium-Low** | 1 | 4 | 4 | 7 |
| **Medium** | 2 | 2 | 8 | 8 |
| **Medium-High** | 3 | 5 | 5 | 9 |
| **High** | 3 | 6 | 6 | 9 |

: Recreation site ranking (columns are environmental score) {#tbl-ranking}

### Recreation from Home Visits

**Distance-banded allocation.** Each population pixel's expected annual trips are shared out among the sites it can reach. Total demand is conserved: a pixel near several sites makes no more trips than an otherwise identical pixel near one site. Demand follows an exponential distance-decay density $f(d) = b\,e^{-bd}$, with the level of demand set separately by a participation parameter $a$, the expected annual trips per person at zero distance.

The 50 km maximum distance is split into $n = 8$ rings. For population pixel $i$, ring $k$ receives a fixed budget of

$$
\text{Pop}_i \cdot a \cdot \text{share}_k, \qquad \text{share}_k = F(d_k) - F(d_{k-1})
$$

This budget depends only on distance. If the ring contains one or more sites, the budget is split evenly among them. If it contains none, that part of the budget is recorded as **unmet demand**. Demand beyond 50 km, $1 - F(50)$, is also unmet:

$$
\text{visits}_{i \to j} = \frac{\text{Pop}_i \cdot a \cdot \text{share}_k}{|\mathcal{S}_k(i)|}, \quad j \in \mathcal{S}_k(i);
\qquad
\sum_j \text{visits}_{i \to j} + \text{unmet}_i = \text{Pop}_i \cdot a
$$

We use a single 50 km cutoff everywhere, rather than one derived from $b$, because $b$ describes how demand is spread across nearby sites, not where day trips physically stop. Fifty kilometres matches the largest distance bin in the calibration surveys (about 46 km on average). With $b = 0.167$/km, $F(50) \approx 99.98\%$, so the cutoff almost never binds.

**Calibration.** We reviewed public surveys of trip frequency and trip distance and kept those that (1) include a "zero visits" category, so that a true per-capita rate can be computed, and (2) separately report how far visitors travel. Three studies met both conditions: the People and Nature Survey for England [@PaNSEngland], a survey of urban nature visits in Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel [@TalalGruntman2023], and a park-visitor survey in Beijing, China [@Tu2020126689]. For each study, $a$ is the mean annual number of visits per person, including people who made none. $b$ is the inverse of the mean travel distance, which is the maximum-likelihood estimate for an exponential distribution. The three studies are averaged without weights, so the very large English sample does not dominate.

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| $a$ (participation) | 102.50 visits/capita/year |
| $b$ (distance decay) | 0.167 /km (mean trip distance $\approx$ 6.0 km) |

: Calibrated demand parameters {#tbl-calibrated-params}

The model can assign different parameters to different groups of countries. With only three usable studies, however, one global pair is applied to all countries. A U.S. survey of visits to other wildlife refuges [@FWSNVS] has a zero-visits category but no distance data. Its much lower rate ($a \approx 4.1$) reflects a narrower definition of a site, so we left it out.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Calibrated distance-decay function"
#| label: fig-distance-decay

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

b = 0.167
d_cutoff = 50
d = np.linspace(0, d_cutoff, 500)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5))
axes[0].plot(d, b * np.exp(-b * d), color='#2c7fb8', linewidth=2)
axes[0].axvline(d_cutoff, color='#666', linestyle='--', linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel('Distance (km)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('$f(d) = b \\cdot e^{-bd}$')
axes[0].set_title('Distance-decay density')
axes[1].plot(d, 1 - np.exp(-b * d), color='#2c7fb8', linewidth=2)
axes[1].axvline(d_cutoff, color='#666', linestyle='--', linewidth=1)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Distance (km)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('$F(d) = 1 - e^{-bd}$')
axes[1].set_title('Cumulative share of demand')
axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Population.** Resident population comes from WorldPop 2020 [@WorldPopUnconstrainedGlobalMosaics2000_2020], aligned to a 0.01° grid. That alignment resampled 30 arc-second counts without rescaling them for the change in pixel area, so we multiply each pixel by $(0.01 / (30/3600))^2 = 1.44$. This brings the world total to 7.97 billion.

### Recreation from Lodging Visits

Tourist visits use the same allocation model. The population input is replaced by each pixel's overnight stays, and the participation rate becomes $a/365$, which turns visits per person per year into visits per visitor-night. National overnight stays (UNWTO, domestic and international) [@UNWTO2023] are spread across each country in proportion to the Delta Check hotel points [@DeltaCheck2023].

UNWTO does not report the overnights indicator for every country in every year. For each country we use the reporting year closest to 2019, but no more than five years away. Countries with no overnights data in that window have missing lodging and accommodation values, not zeros.

### Overnight Stays and Arrivals

Accommodation is priced on the same national overnight-stay totals, allocated to pixels as above. Air travel is priced on international arrivals by origin region, $A_r$, from UNWTO's arrivals-by-region-of-origin indicator [@UNWTO2023]. This indicator is reported separately from overnights, so the two components can cover different sets of countries.

The arrivals indicator counts all arrivals by every mode of transport. To isolate air travel we multiply by each country's share of arrivals that come by air, $s^{\text{air}}$. This share is the ratio of air to total arrivals in UNWTO's transport table, using the year closest to 2019 within five years. The share is measured directly for 173 countries. For the other 76 it is set to their UNWTO region's median, or the global median when the region has no data, and these cases are flagged in the output.

### Data Harmonization

- **Units.** UNWTO tourism figures are reported in thousands and are converted to counts.
- **Country codes.** UNWTO uses older M49 codes for some countries, such as 280 for Germany and older codes for several Caribbean territories. We recode these to the country IDs used throughout the pipeline, and sum codes that merge into one country.
- **Grid geometry.** The grid uses geographic coordinates, so a pixel's east-west width shrinks by $\cos(\text{latitude})$. Distance kernels are built as ellipses using the pixel width at each tile's latitude.

## Estimating Price

### Ground Travel

Visits allocated to ring $k$ are priced at the round-trip fuel cost to the ring's midpoint, $\bar{d}_k$:

$$
\text{value}_{i \to j} = \text{visits}_{i \to j} \times c_i \times 2\bar{d}_k
$$

$c_i$ is the fuel cost per kilometre in the traveller's origin country [@GlobalPetrolPrices2025; @IEA2020FuelPrices; @IEA2021GFEI]. For lodging visits, this is the country where the tourist is staying. Midpoint pricing matches the way budgets are allocated, by distance alone. The price assumes car travel and counts fuel only: it leaves out the value of travel time and other vehicle costs, so it is a lower bound. Fuel costs are missing for 81 of the 250 countries. Those countries still get visit counts, but their value is reported as missing.

### Accommodation

Accommodation value is the number of overnight stays times the hotel price per person per night, calculated for each pixel. Hotel prices come from a gap-filled global price surface [@GlobalHotelPriceGrid2026]:

- **Source.** The surface is built from hotel-booking rate quotes, averaged to a 0.5° grid as a mean price per person per night. Each hotel gets equal weight.
- **Gap-filling.** Only 8.3% of land cells are observed directly. The rest are filled by kriging on log prices, then by the nearest observed cell within 500 km, then by the country mean. This raises coverage to 73.7% of land.
- **Why the mean.** We use mean prices because their sum gives total spending.

Cells still without a price are treated as missing, not free. This affects 1 of the 143,340 pixels that have allocated stays.

### Air Travel

Air travel value is the number of arrivals from each origin region that came by air, times the fare from that region:

$$
\text{air}_R = \sum_r A_r \, s^{\text{air}}_R \, \text{fare}_{r \to R}
$$

Countries are assigned to UNWTO's seven tourism regions, which differ in places from continental groupings. For example, Egypt and Libya are in the Middle East, and Turkey, Cyprus and the Caucasus are in Europe. Fares come from a single flight-search survey [@flightlist_2026]:

- **Coverage.** 18 hub airports (3 per region) and 306 ordered hub pairs.
- **Fare per pair.** The mean of the 5 cheapest round-trip quotes, averaged up to region pairs.
- **Snapshot.** Searches were run in September 2026 for October 2026 departures. The results are stored as a fixed input so the scrape is not re-run.
- **Deflation to 2019.** Fares are multiplied by the 2019 average of the U.S. CPI-U Airline Fares index divided by its value in the survey month (factor 0.840) [@BLSAirlineCPI].

Arrivals from the residual "Other" region are counted but not priced.

## Lambda

We need a share $\lambda$ for the portion of value that can be credited to nature. It differs by component:

- **Ground travel ($\lambda = 1$).** These trips are already limited to high-quality nature sites, so the whole trip cost counts as nature-attributable. This puts all of the attribution in the site definition. It also ignores the built infrastructure, such as roads, trails and parking, that makes access possible.
- **Accommodation and air travel ($\lambda = 0.183$, applied to personal travel only).** Hotel stays and flights serve many purposes. We first keep only personal (non-business) travel, using each country's share of inbound arrivals by purpose, $s^{\text{personal}}$, from UNWTO [@UNWTO2023]. That share is measured for 168 countries and filled with the regional median for the other 81; the median is 0.87. We then scale by the share of personal travellers who name "natural environment" as the main reason for choosing their destination. That share is 18.3%, the EU-27 average in Flash Eurobarometer 499 [@Eurobarometer499], applied as one global value. The attribution for these two components is therefore $s^{\text{personal}} \times \lambda$.

Both steps are needed because the Eurobarometer share applies only to people travelling for personal reasons. A business trip is not counted as nature-motivated even when the destination is.

**Sensitivity.** The value of $\lambda$ has a large effect on the total.

| $\lambda$ | Basis | Accommodation + air (USD) |
|---|---|---|
| **0.183** | Nature as the *main* reason for choosing a destination (Eurobarometer 499) | **~\$231B** |
| 0.426 | Nature as one of the top two reasons (Eurobarometer 499) | ~\$538B |

: Sensitivity of results to $\lambda$ (before attribution: accommodation \$1,010B, air \$445B) {#tbl-lambda}

Country-level values before attribution are kept in the output (`*_uncapped` columns).

## Variables and Datasets

| Variable | Dataset | Source | Resolution |
|----------|---------|--------|------------|
| Land cover | ESA-CCI Land Cover | [@ESA2017LandCoverCCI] | 300m |
| Protected areas | World Database on Protected Areas | [@UNEPWCMC_WDPA] | Vector |
| Road density | GRIP4 Global Roads | [@Meijer2018] | Vector |
| Population | WorldPop 2020 | [@WorldPopUnconstrainedGlobalMosaics2000_2020] | 1km |
| Overnight stays, arrivals, transport mode | UNWTO Tourism Statistics | [@UNWTO2023] | Country |
| Accommodation points | Delta Check Hotel Database | [@DeltaCheck2023] | Points |
| Hotel prices | Global Hotel Price Grid (gap-filled) | [@GlobalHotelPriceGrid2026] | 0.5° |
| Fuel costs | Country fuel price data | [@GlobalPetrolPrices2025; @IEA2020FuelPrices; @IEA2021GFEI] | Country |
| Airfares | Flight search survey (Sep 2026) | [@flightlist_2026] | Region pairs |
| Airfare deflator | CPI-U Airline Fares (CUUR0000SETG01) | [@BLSAirlineCPI] | US, monthly |
| Demand parameters | Trip-frequency and distance surveys | [@PaNSEngland; @TalalGruntman2023; @Tu2020126689] | Single global group |
| Nature-attribution share | Flash Eurobarometer 499 | [@Eurobarometer499] | EU-27 |

: Key variables and datasets {#tbl-datasets}

## Validation

We compared recreation-from-home results with the JRC INCA outdoor recreation account [@Vallecillo2019196], which reports 2012 visits to high-quality areas in 28 European countries.

- **Ranking.** Our country rankings closely match JRC's. Across the 28 countries the Spearman correlation is 0.96 ($p < 0.001$).
- **Scale.** Our visit counts are about 1,000 times JRC's (median; the range is 660–1,930). JRC records 40 million visits across the 28 countries, about 0.09 per person per year; we record 41 billion. This gap comes from two differences in scope. JRC counts only walking and cycling within 4 km. We count car trips up to 50 km, with participation calibrated on surveys that ask about visits to "any park or green space".
- **Value per visit.** Our value is about USD 1.37 per visit across these countries, compared with EUR 1,256 in JRC's account, so ours is roughly 900 times lower. JRC values trips with a zonal travel-cost demand curve; we count fuel spending only.
- **Total value.** The two gaps roughly cancel. Our total is USD 57B; JRC's is EUR 50B, roughly equal at 2012 exchange rates. That match is a coincidence of offsetting differences, not a confirmation of either level.

The JRC figures come from the INCA outdoor recreation GeoPackage (LAU level, 2012), with LAU totals summed to countries. The JRC value per visit is the figure published in @Vallecillo2019196.

These checks show that the model's spatial pattern is right. They do not test the absolute number of visits or their value.

## Limitations

- **Site definition favours some regions.** Global class breaks in the environmental index leave very few high-quality sites in parts of South and East Asia:
  - Only 0.2% of land counts as a site in China and India, against 15–23% in Western Europe and Japan.
  - As a result, 98–99% of their daily demand is unmet, against 80% worldwide.
  - Lowering the threshold to class 8 or 7 does not fix this.
  - Their daily values should be read as lower bounds. Setting class breaks by region is a candidate fix.
- **Missing overnights data.** Brazil, China, Indonesia, Thailand, India and others have no usable UNWTO overnights figures, so their accommodation value is missing.
- **US domestic overnights.** These are not in the UNWTO data, so US accommodation value is understated.
- **Price is a lower bound.** Ground travel counts fuel only, with no value of travel time.
- **One global $\lambda$.** It comes from EU survey data, and the right share likely varies by destination.
- **Same-day visitors.** For some countries the arrivals figures include them.
- **One global set of demand parameters.** Only three surveys qualified. Country- or region-specific parameters need independent visitation data that is resolved geographically. The model's own simulated (distance, cost, visits) triples cannot be used for this, because they are generated from the parameters themselves.

# Results

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| label: imports

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown
from tabulate import tabulate

def format_abbreviated(x):
    """Adaptive K/M/B/T abbreviation, e.g. 742,300 -> '742.3K', 6.8e9 -> '6.8B'.
    Used for both map colorbars and the country results table so magnitudes
    spanning thousands to hundreds of billions stay comparably legible,
    rather than a single fixed unit (e.g. millions) leaving small countries
    as indistinguishable 0.0s."""
    if pd.isna(x):
        return ''
    sign = '-' if x < 0 else ''
    abs_x = abs(x)
    if abs_x >= 1e12:
        return f"{sign}{abs_x / 1e12:.1f}T"
    if abs_x >= 1e9:
        return f"{sign}{abs_x / 1e9:.1f}B"
    if abs_x >= 1e6:
        return f"{sign}{abs_x / 1e6:.1f}M"
    if abs_x >= 1e3:
        return f"{sign}{abs_x / 1e3:.1f}K"
    return f"{sign}{abs_x:.0f}"
```

```{python}
# Drop Antarctica for clarity

# Rename columns for clarity
gdf = gdf.rename(columns={
    'daily_visits': 'home_visits',
    'daily_value': 'home_value',
    'tourist_visits': 'lodging_visits',
    'tourist_value': 'lodging_value'
})

# Combined totals. total_value is ground travel only (home + lodging).
# grand_total_value comes from the pipeline: all four components, with
# lambda applied to accommodation and air travel, summed over the
# components that are available (NaN only if all four are missing).
gdf['total_visits'] = gdf['home_visits'] + gdf['lodging_visits']
gdf['total_value'] = gdf['home_value'] + gdf['lodging_value']
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 4))
gdf.plot(column="lodging_value", ax=ax, legend=True, cmap="Greens", 
         edgecolor='none', legend_kwds={'shrink': 0.5})
ax.set_title("Global Recreation from Lodging Value (USD)", fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_axis_off()
format_cbar_with_commas(ax)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Results by Country

```{python}
#| label: tbl-country-results
#| tbl-cap: "Country-Level Recreation Results (Sorted by Grand Total Value)"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

# Create summary table
summary_df = gdf.drop(columns='geometry')[[
  'iso3_r250_label',
  'home_visits',
  'home_value',
  'lodging_visits',
  'lodging_value',
  'accommodation_value',
  'air_travel_value',
  'total_visits',
  'total_value',
  'grand_total_value']]

# Sort by grand total value (all four components, lambda applied)
summary_df = summary_df.sort_values('grand_total_value', ascending=False)

# Rename columns for display. "Ground Travel Value" (not "Total Value") is
# deliberately not adjacent to "Grand Total Value" in meaning even though it
# sits next to it in the table -- it is only home + lodging value, excluding
# accommodation and air travel; "Grand Total Value" is the true sum of all
# four value components.
summary_df = summary_df.rename(columns={
    'iso3_r250_label': 'Country',
    'home_visits': 'Recreation from Home Visits',
    'home_value': 'Recreation from Home Value (USD)',
    'lodging_visits': 'Recreation from Lodging Visits',
    'lodging_value': 'Recreation from Lodging Value (USD)',
    'accommodation_value': 'Accommodation Value (USD)',
    'air_travel_value': 'Air Travel Value (USD)',
    'total_visits': 'Total Visits',
    'total_value': 'Ground Travel Value (Home + Lodging, USD)',
    'grand_total_value': 'Grand Total Value (USD)'
})

# Format large numbers with adaptive K/M/B/T abbreviations (see format_abbreviated
# in the imports cell), so magnitudes from thousands to hundreds of billions
# stay comparably legible rather than all-digit strings of varying length
for col in summary_df.columns[1:]:
    summary_df[col] = summary_df[col].apply(format_abbreviated)

# Display using markdown for better Word compatibility
Markdown(tabulate(summary_df, headers='keys', tablefmt='pipe', showindex=False))
```
